title: Vau calculus, explained
h1: Vau calculus: fexprs with a real equational theory, because evaluation is explicit
lead: In Lisp, a fexpr is a first-class combiner that receives its operands unevaluated. Mitchell Wand showed in 1998 that in his calculus, where evaluation is implicit (every reduction is evaluation) and fexprs are fully reflective, contextual equivalence is trivial. John N. Shutt's vau calculi avoid this by making evaluation explicit: a term [eval T] asks for evaluation, and the operand T alone is just data. This site explains the pure vau-x calculus (Shutt's thesis, section 9.3) and a Lean 4 formalization of it in this repository, with no sorry. Four headlines are proved in Lean for the concrete vau-x rules: evaluation is a special case of reduction, vau-x conservatively extends the call-by-value lambda calculus, the rules are confluent, and contextual equivalence is nontrivial. A fifth, derived $lambda, needs environments and is still a PLAN. The Lean does not formalize Shutt's general framework of regular substitutive reduction systems.
desc: Unofficial, AI-drafted explainer of John N. Shutt's vau calculus with a Lean 4 formalization of the pure vau-x calculus (no sorry, no Mathlib): syntax, de Bruijn substitution, the seven reduction rules, compatible closure, and four proved headlines: evaluation is reduction, conservative extension of call-by-value lambda, confluence, and nontrivial contextual equivalence. Derived $lambda and environments are planned.
startIntro: The headline statements, then every definition you need to read them, simplest first. Four headlines are proved in Lean (no sorry); DerivedLambda is still a PLAN and claims nothing.
startNote: All definitions follow Shutt's PhD thesis (WPI, 2010), chapter 9: the pure vau-x calculus of section 9.3, and, only to make $vau understandable, the environment calculus vau-e of section 9.1. The Lean (folder Vau/) uses de Bruijn indices for variables and has no delta-rules. In the text, notation is ASCII: [eval T], [combine T1 T2], <T> for an applicative, and <vau x.T>, <vau0.T>, <vau2.T> for the three compound operatives. The rule names (eval-self and so on) are this project's names for Shutt's schemata (9.25S), (9.25p), (9.25a), (9.25gamma), (9.25beta), (9.25vau0) and (9.25vau2).
sizeNote: Step 3: Lean 4 formalization of vau-x in Vau/ (7 files, no sorry, no axiom declarations). 4 headlines proved, 1 planned. Nodes without Lean are marked PLAN.

aboutCreditMd:
## Credit, licence and status

- **The theory:** the vau calculi are the work of [John N. Shutt](https://web.cs.wpi.edu/~jshutt/), in his PhD thesis *Fexprs as the basis of Lisp function application; or, $vau: the ultimate abstraction* (Worcester Polytechnic Institute, 2010) and his 2007 NEPLS talk. The actor view of Kernel is from Dale Schumacher's posts. The triviality result is from Mitchell Wand, *The Theory of Fexprs is Trivial* (Lisp and Symbolic Computation, 1998).
- **This explainer and its Lean:** unofficial and independent. Drafted by Claude (AI) at the request of the repository owner. No person has reviewed them, and the cited authors have not seen them. Every node is `review: draft`.
- **Lean:** folder `Vau/`, Lean 4 v4.32.2, no Mathlib, no `sorry`, no `axiom` declarations. See the [Trust](#/trust) page for the `#print axioms` output of each headline.
- **Licence:** this repository is under the [MIT License](https://github.com/tangentproofs/vau-calculus/blob/main/LICENSE). The cited works keep their own copyright. This site quotes only short, attributed phrases and does not copy the thesis.
- **Corrections:** open an issue or pull request on [tangentproofs/vau-calculus](https://github.com/tangentproofs/vau-calculus), or comment on any node.
